items.abstract: <jats:p>Graph classification is a challenging research task in many applications across a broad range of domains. Recently, Graph Neural Network (GNN) models have achieved superior performance on various real-world graph datasets. Despite their successes, most of current GNN models largely suffer from the ubiquitous class imbalance problem, which typically results in prediction bias towards majority classes. Although many imbalanced learning methods have been proposed, they mainly focus on regular Euclidean data and cannot well utilize topological structure of graph (non-Euclidean) data.  To boost the performance of GNNs and investigate the relationship between topological structure and class imbalance, we propose GraphDIVE, which learns multi-view graph representations and combine multi-view experts (i.e., classifiers). Specifically, multi-view graph representations correspond to the intrinsic diverse graph topological structure characteristics. Extensive experiments on molecular benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.</jats:p>
title: GraphDIVE: Graph Classification by Mixture of Diverse Experts

items.abstract: <jats:p>Fair graph node classification aims to reduce the dependence of predictions on sensitive attributes while preserving predictive utility. However, many existing methods rely on a shared representation path for fairness and utility, which may couple potentially competing objectives. In addition, fairness-oriented modeling is often centered on local neighborhoods, which may overlook fairness-related information from broader structural contexts. To address these issues, we propose FairMoE, a mixture-of-experts framework for fair graph node classification. FairMoE functionally separates the two objectives through a Fairness Expert Group and a Utility Expert Group, which respectively perform fairness-oriented and utility-oriented learning. Within the Fairness Expert Group, multiple Fairness Experts operate over different receptive fields to learn fairness-oriented representations from local and higher-order structural contexts. In parallel, the Utility Expert Group employs complementary experts to preserve task-discriminative information. The two outputs are then coordinated by a Dynamic Gate, which produces node-specific weights to control how much utility information supplements the fairness-oriented prediction. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that FairMoE achieves a competitive trade-off between fairness and classification utility, with particularly strong results on fairness metrics. Further ablation and structural analyses support the effectiveness of the core designs. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.</jats:p>
title: FairMoE:A Functionally Specialized Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Fair Graph Node Classification
